title: It started with a graduate student who hurt his wrists typing his own dissertation.
description:
It started with a graduate student who hurt his wrists typing his own dissertation. Wayne Westerman was finishing a PhD on multi-touch surfaces at the University of Delaware when repetitive strain problems pushed him toward low-impact ways of typing.

founded FingerWorks at the University of Delaware to build multi-touch keyboards and pads aimed at people with RSI.

He wanted computers to feel as expressive as playing the piano. His own words: he had an ergonomic problem and paired it with a motivation, wanting to pull some of a piano's grace into the computer experience.

Apple bought FingerWorks in early 2005, taking the patents, the products and both founders. FingerWorks stopped shipping and closed that June. Outside customers only learned a big company had bought them; nobody said which one, or why, for two more years.

The iPhone did not arrive until 2007. Its touchscreen came from a keyboard built for sore wrists.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FingerWorks: FingerWorks was founded in 1998 by Wayne Westerman and John Elias at the University of Delaware; Apple acquired the company's assets, patents and both founders in early 2005, and the technology became the basis for the iPhone's touchscreen, launched in 2007.
- https://www.macrumors.com/2009/02/18/apples-multi-touch-designer-describes-his-inspiration-more-to-come/: relays a University of Delaware news article in which Westerman describes developing repetitive strain problems while finishing his dissertation, and says he wanted computers to feel as expressive as playing the piano.
